markingScheme.criterion: States that the computer would not work at all — it could not think, calculate, run programs, or process anything.
markingScheme.accept: 'Freezes', 'won't turn on/work', 'does nothing' or similar — any description that nothing at all can be processed.
markingScheme.insufficient: 'It would run slower' — that describes a different problem (like low RAM), not a fully broken CPU.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains this is because the CPU is the computer's 'brain' that processes instructions, and every other part depends on it to work.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent wording such as 'the part that does the thinking/calculating' — the exact word 'CPU' does not need repeating.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that having power, memory and a working screen would not matter, because none of them can do anything without the CPU processing instructions.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'the computer would still work a bit' — this misses that nothing at all is possible without the CPU.

markingScheme.criterion: Identifies RAM and/or a faster CPU as the part(s) to upgrade for the 'programs take ages to open' problem.
markingScheme.accept: Naming RAM (more working memory), CPU (a faster processor), or both.
markingScheme.insufficient: Naming a part with no link to the slow-opening problem, e.g. the case.

markingScheme.criterion: Identifies the graphics card as the part to upgrade for the 'blocky, slow-looking games' problem.
markingScheme.insufficient: Suggesting an unrelated part for the graphics problem.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains, for at least one of the two parts named, why that part's job matches the specific symptom described (e.g. RAM/CPU handle what is running, so more/faster helps programs open quickly; the graphics card draws what appears on screen, so a better one stops blocky, slow graphics).
markingScheme.insufficient: Naming correct parts with no explanation of why they fix the symptom.

levels.descriptor: Achieves none of the three points: does not say the computer would stop working at all, does not explain that the CPU is the 'brain' that processes instructions, and does not explain that the other parts wouldn't matter without it.

Achieves only ONE of the three: says the computer would stop working completely OR explains that the CPU is the part that thinks/processes instructions OR explains that power, memory and the screen wouldn't matter without it — the other two points are missing.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. says the computer would stop working and explains that the CPU is the part that thinks/processes instructions, but does not go on to explain that power, memory and a working screen wouldn't matter without it (or reaches that final point without clearly establishing the CPU's role first).

Achieves all three: says the computer would stop working completely, explains that the CPU is the part that thinks/processes instructions and every other part depends on it, and explains that power, memory and a working screen would not matter because nothing can be processed without the CPU.

criteria.source: = the Apply question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one. Do not award these marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: Achieves none of the three points: no correct part named for the slow-programs problem, no correct part named for the blocky-games problem, and no explanation of why any named part's job fixes either symptom.

Achieves only ONE of the three: names RAM and/or a faster CPU for the slow-programs problem OR names the graphics card for the blocky-games problem OR explains why a correctly-named part's job fixes a symptom — the other two are missing or incorrect.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. correctly names RAM/CPU for slow programs AND the graphics card for blocky games, but does not go on to explain why either part's job fixes its symptom (or names one part correctly and explains why it fixes its symptom, but the other part is missing or wrong).

Achieves all three: names RAM and/or a faster CPU for the slow-programs problem, names the graphics card for the blocky-games problem, and explains why at least one of those parts' jobs fixes its specific symptom.
